hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
In a nursing home filled with people in their 90s—many too frail to walk without help or stand up from a chair on their own—researchers decided to put them on a weight-training program.
Not light calisthenics. Not gentle stretching. High-intensity progressive resistance training, three times a week, with loads that eventually reached about 80% of each person’s maximum. The results, published in JAMA in 1990 by Maria Fiatarone and colleagues, upended long-held assumptions about aging and muscle.
Ten frail, institutionalized volunteers (average age 90, some as old as 96) trained their quadriceps for just eight weeks. Their strength exploded—an average gain of 174%, with some individuals more than tripling their starting numbers. Mid-thigh muscle cross-sectional area increased by roughly 9%. More importantly, function improved: tandem gait speed rose nearly 50%. Several participants who had needed canes or arm support to rise from a chair no longer did. Attendance was extraordinarily high; these were not people who were easily motivated by abstract health advice, yet they showed up and pushed themselves.
The study demonstrated something radical for its time: the muscles of people in their tenth decade still possess remarkable plasticity. They respond to progressive overload with substantial gains in strength, size, and real-world mobility—changes that meaningfully restored independence and reduced the burden of frailty. The relative magnitude of adaptation was comparable to what much younger adults experience under similar training.
In short, the experiment proved that chronological age, even extreme age accompanied by chronic disease and institutionalization, does not erase the body’s capacity to grow stronger. Strength training could reverse a large portion of the functional decline once considered inevitable.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Shawn Baker dug up a 1990 study from JAMA. Researchers put frail nursing-home residents, average age 90, on proper weight training three times a week, working up to about 80% of their max.

In eight weeks their leg strength went up 174% on average. Walking speed improved by nearly half, and a few who'd needed a cane or a hand to get out of a chair didn't anymore.

If muscle still answers at 90, it'll answer at 50 or 60. It's never too late to start. Start light, build up slowly, and get your GP's tick first if you've got a heart or joint problem.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
For decades, plant-based advocates insisted saturated fat was a dietary poison that clogged arteries and shortened lives. Then one of the largest nutrition studies ever conducted arrived and refused to cooperate.
The Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology (PURE) study followed 135,335 adults aged 35–70 from 18 countries spanning five continents—high-, middle-, and low-income nations alike. Over a median of 7.4 years, researchers documented nearly 5,800 deaths and almost 4,800 major cardiovascular events. Diets were assessed with food-frequency questionnaires, and participants were grouped by quintiles of carbohydrate and fat intake.
The results, published in The Lancet in 2017, upended conventional wisdom. Higher total fat intake was linked to a 23% lower risk of total mortality. Saturated fat specifically showed an inverse association: those in the highest quintile had a 14% lower risk of dying from any cause compared with the lowest quintile, plus a reduced risk of stroke. Total fat and saturated fat showed no significant link to myocardial infarction or cardiovascular death. By contrast, the highest carbohydrate intakes were associated with a 28% higher risk of total mortality.
The authors noted that these findings stood in contrast to longstanding dietary guidelines that had demonized saturated fat. The sheer scale and geographic diversity of PURE made the results hard to dismiss as a niche Western phenomenon.
Plant-based advocates and low-fat proponents reacted with urgency. Critiques poured out from academic nutrition centers and plant-focused organizations, emphasizing confounding by poverty (high-carb diets in poorer regions), the limitations of observational data, and self-reported intake. Some argued the study changed nothing or was misleading. The intensity of the pushback underscored how directly PURE challenged decades of messaging that had elevated plant foods while casting animal fats as uniquely harmful.
In a field long dominated by consensus rather than consistent outcome data, PURE’s size and findings forced a reckoning: saturated fat was not the mortality risk it had been portrayed to be.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Shawn Baker pointed back to the PURE study: 135,000 adults in 18 countries, followed for about seven years, published in The Lancet in 2017.

Higher total fat was linked to a 23% lower risk of dying, and the people eating the most saturated fat had a 14% lower risk than those eating the least. The highest carb intakes were linked to a 28% higher risk.

It's observational, and critics point out high-carb diets are more common in poorer countries, so it's a link, not proof. But it's a fair reason not to fear eggs, meat and butter on a working plate. If you've got heart trouble, talk it through with your doctor.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
India’s Olympic medal haul is abysmal even by the standards of other poor countries—and the near-total absence of meat in the national diet is a major, under-discussed factor.
All-time, India has roughly 41 Olympic medals. China has ~817. Kenya and Ethiopia, far poorer on average, regularly dominate distance running. Cuba, despite decades of poverty and isolation, has punched far above its weight in boxing, baseball, and track. Even small, resource-constrained nations have produced more consistent elite results relative to population and income than India has. 
In the early 1980s, when both China and India had extremely high poverty rates, China returned to the Olympics and immediately finished 4th with 32 medals (15 gold). India won nothing in 1984 and 1988. The gap has persisted as both countries grew richer.
Meat supply per person in India is among the lowest in the world—roughly 4–8 kg per year. China is 8–15 times higher. Most other countries that outperform India in strength, power, and team sports eat far more animal protein. India’s diet is dominated by grains, pulses, and dairy; meat is culturally and economically marginal for the majority of the population.
This shows up in athletic outcomes. Low animal-protein intake is linked to lower lean mass, slower recovery, reduced strength and power output, higher rates of anemia (especially iron-deficiency), and poorer bone density—exactly the traits that limit performance in the sports that produce the most Olympic medals. Endurance events in East Africa succeed on high-carb diets, but the rest of the Olympic program (weightlifting, wrestling, sprinting, throwing, team sports, combat sports) rewards animal protein. India’s historical strength was field hockey; individual power and strength sports have lagged for generations.
India’s recent Asian Games improvements are real, but the Olympic numbers remain tiny relative to 1.4 billion people. Until animal-protein availability rises substantially for ordinary athletes—not just the elite few in national camps—the medal table is unlikely to change in any meaningful way. Poverty alone does not explain it. Plenty of poorer places have done better.

Higher meat intake tracks with longer lives—and the usual “plant-based is better” story collapses under population data.
Across 175 countries, total meat supply (all flesh meats and offal, grams per person per day from FAO data, 2011–2013 averages) showed a strong positive correlation with life expectancy at birth (Pearson r ≈ 0.710) and at age 5, plus a clear inverse link with under-5 child mortality (r ≈ −0.746). Carbohydrate crops (cereals, starchy roots, and sugars) showed only a weak, non-significant or negative association. Meat intake explained at least half the variance in the key scatterplots. These patterns held across developed and developing countries, most WHO regions, and both high- and low-meat groups. 
The authors directly tested the usual confounders that plant-based advocates often cite. Partial correlations kept the meat–life-expectancy relationship significant after controlling for total caloric intake, urbanization, GDP (purchasing-power parity), adult obesity prevalence, and carbohydrate-crop intake. Stepwise linear regression selected meat—not carbohydrate crops—as a significant independent predictor. Education level was also examined where data allowed. In short, the association did not disappear once wealth, energy balance, city living, obesity, or carbohydrate volume were held constant. The researchers noted that many vegetarian longevity studies suffer from non-representative samples (e.g., health-conscious Adventists) and incomplete lifestyle adjustment; their broader ecological approach was designed to reduce that bias.
This is population-level ecological evidence, not proof of individual causation, and residual factors (healthcare quality, sanitation, smoking, activity, genetics, food processing) remain possible. Still, it undercuts the narrative that simply swapping meat for grains and plants reliably extends life. High-meat traditional pastoral cultures (Mongolian nomads, certain Arctic and African herding groups) contrast with long-standing cereal-dominant agricultural societies where meat was scarcer; the global data align more with the former pattern than with modern low-meat prescriptions.

When the editor of the world’s most prestigious medical journal concluded that much of the clinical research it published could no longer be trusted, the problem was no longer abstract.
Marcia Angell, a pathologist who joined the New England Journal of Medicine staff in 1979, rose to executive editor and then served as interim editor-in-chief from 1999 to June 2000. She stepped down after more than two decades at the journal, formally to write a book. The deeper context was her growing conviction, formed from years of editing manuscripts, that pharmaceutical industry influence had compromised the independence of clinical research. She and previous editors had enforced strict conflict-of-interest rules, yet industry-sponsored studies continued to arrive with designs, analyses, and selective reporting that favored the sponsor’s product. Negative results were often suppressed, side effects minimized, and “academic” authors frequently carried undisclosed financial ties. 
In a widely cited 2009 New York Review of Books essay, Angell wrote the line that crystallized her position: “It is simply no longer possible to believe much of the clinical research that is published, or to rely on the judgment of trusted physicians or authoritative medical guidelines. I take no pleasure in this conclusion, which I reached slowly and reluctantly over my two decades as an editor of The New England Journal of Medicine.” She described an industry that had shifted from discovering useful drugs toward marketing, co-opting academic medical centers, researchers, and even the journals that were supposed to serve as independent arbiters. Her 2000 editorial “Is Academic Medicine for Sale?” and later book The Truth About the Drug Companies expanded the critique, arguing that commercial priorities systematically distorted what research was done, how it was conducted, and what reached publication. 
Angell’s departure marked the end of an era of tighter editorial resistance to industry influence at the NEJM. Her public statements afterward made clear that she viewed the problem as systemic rather than isolated: once the bulk of clinical research depended on commercial funding, journals could no longer function as reliable filters of medical evidence.

For nearly two million years, the dominant story of human evolution wasn’t one of flexible omnivores cleverly mixing plants and animals. It was the rise of specialized hypercarnivorous apex predators whose bodies, genes, and behavior were built around hunting large, fat-rich animals—and whose biology still carries that signature today.
In their 2021 paper “The Evolution of the Human Trophic Level During the Pleistocene” (American Journal of Physical Anthropology), Miki Ben-Dor, Raphaël Sirtoli, and Ran Barkai reconstruct what humans actually ate during the Pleistocene without relying on the usual ethnographic analogies to recent hunter-gatherers (whose environments and prey bases were radically different). 
They assembled 25 independent lines of evidence drawn from human physiology and genetics, archaeology, paleontology, and zoology. The cumulative picture is clear: the Homo lineage shifted from a lower trophic level toward a high, carnivorous position beginning with Homo habilis, peaking with Homo erectus, and remaining elevated for most of the Pleistocene. Humans functioned as social hunters of large prey (megafauna and large mammals) and, by comparison with modern social carnivores, as hypercarnivores deriving roughly 70% or more of their calories from animal sources. 
Key categories of evidence include:
•  Physiology and metabolism: Human stomach acidity is unusually high—even compared with other predators—consistent with consuming meat that could sit for days (as from large kills). Genetic patterns show adaptations favoring a fat-rich animal diet in humans while chimpanzees show the opposite shift toward sugars.
•  Archaeology and stable isotopes: Multiple stable-isotope studies of prehistoric human remains indicate high animal-protein diets until late in the Paleolithic. Zooarchaeology shows repeated targeting of large herbivores, with early access to high-ranking prey.
•  Paleontology and ecology: Humans entered and competed within the large-predator guild; prey-size decline later tracked changes in human morphology, technology, and diet. Large animals provided the fat and caloric density that smaller, leaner prey could not match efficiently.
•  Zoological analogy: Social carnivores that hunt large prey are hypercarnivores; the human pattern of large-prey specialization aligns with this category.
A reversal toward lower trophic levels appears in the Upper Paleolithic, strengthens in the Mesolithic/Epipaleolithic and Neolithic, and culminates with agriculture. The authors emphasize that modern human genetics, metabolism, and morphology still retain “the memory of an adaptation to a trophic level” that was predominantly carnivorous for the great majority of the Pleistocene. 
This multidisciplinary approach—twenty-five convergent lines rather than a single analogy—offers one of the more robust reconstructions of ancestral human diet available. It reframes the long Pleistocene as a period of specialized large-game hunting rather than generalized omnivory, with downstream implications for understanding human brain expansion, morphology, and the later dietary transition driven by declining megafauna.

In 2019, a team of rigorous methodologists—including Gordon Guyatt, the physician who coined the term “evidence-based medicine”—dropped a bombshell: the long-standing claims linking red meat to heart disease and cancer rested on extremely weak evidence.
Published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, the NutriRECS consortium’s series of systematic reviews and guidelines examined roughly 180 observational studies covering millions of people plus the limited randomized trial data available. Using the GRADE framework (which Guyatt helped develop and which is now the standard for rating evidence certainty at organizations like the WHO), the authors rated the evidence linking unprocessed red meat and processed meat to cardiovascular disease, cancer, and mortality as low to very low certainty. Absolute risk reductions from cutting back by three servings per week were tiny and often trivial. The panel therefore issued a weak recommendation that adults continue their current levels of red and processed meat consumption rather than be told to cut back for health reasons.
The authors emphasized transparency: most people value the taste and convenience of meat enough that, given the uncertain and small benefits of reduction, continuing current habits is reasonable. They deliberately excluded animal welfare and environmental concerns, focusing only on human health outcomes.
The reaction from plant-based advocacy groups was swift and aggressive. The Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine (PCRM), a prominent vegan-oriented organization, petitioned the Federal Trade Commission, arguing that the journal’s promotion of the findings was misleading advertising. Groups such as the True Health Initiative also pressed the journal to retract or withhold the papers before publication, citing alleged conflicts and methodological disagreement. Critics highlighted past industry ties of some authors and contended that GRADE was being misapplied to nutrition data. The intensity of the campaign underscored how deeply the weak-evidence conclusion challenged entrenched dietary dogma.
Guyatt and his colleagues stood by the work, arguing that honest assessment of evidence quality—rather than overconfident guidelines based on low-certainty data—better serves the public. The episode remains a stark illustration of how weak observational associations have been treated as settled science on red meat.

Over the past generation and a half, America has quietly lost nearly half its cattle ranchers.
According to USDA Census of Agriculture data and analyses from producer groups such as R-CALF USA, the country has shed more than 650,000–700,000 beef cattle operations since around 1980. What has disappeared are the independent family ranches—especially the smaller and mid-sized ones that once dotted rural landscapes. Most remaining operations are still modest (the majority own fewer than 50 cows), yet the bulk of the national herd is increasingly concentrated in larger herds. The largest operations have grown even as the overall number of ranchers shrinks.
The forces behind the exit are familiar and compounding. Four major packers now control the great majority of beef processing, leaving many ranchers as price-takers in a highly concentrated market. Rising costs for land, feed, labor, equipment, and interest rates have squeezed margins. Prolonged droughts forced herd liquidations. An aging producer base (average age near 58) faces limited succession, while high capital barriers discourage younger entrants. Urban sprawl, regulatory pressures on public lands, and competition from imports have added further pressure.
The result is a quieter countryside: fewer pickup trucks at the sale barn, fewer multi-generational operations passing down knowledge and land, and greater vulnerability in a supply chain that once rested on thousands of independent producers. What if the real key to living longer isn’t just how strong you are—but how fast you can move that strength? A landmark 2025 study in Mayo Clinic Proceedings shows that muscle power (force times velocity) predicts mortality far more powerfully than traditional strength in middle-aged and older adults. 
Researchers from the CLINIMEX Exercise cohort followed 3,889 adults aged 46–75 (roughly two-thirds men) for a median of nearly 11 years. They measured relative muscle power—how much force someone could produce quickly during an upper-row movement, scaled to body weight—and relative strength via a standard handgrip test. After adjusting for age, body composition, and health conditions, the results were striking: people in the lowest power category faced roughly 6–7 times the mortality risk of those in the highest category (hazard ratios of 5.88 for men and 6.90 for women). Strength showed only weak, nonsignificant links to death. 
In other words, the ability to generate force rapidly mattered more for survival than maximal force alone. Power declines faster with age than pure strength, and it underpins everyday tasks that keep people independent—rising quickly from a chair, climbing stairs, recovering from a stumble, or catching yourself in a fall.
Typical athletic activities and tests that demand power include vertical or broad jumps, medicine-ball throws or slams, power cleans or snatches, sprint starts, plyometric hops, and rapid chair rises or sit-to-stands performed as explosively as possible. Even an upright row or push performed at maximum speed (as used in the study) captures the force-velocity product that pure strength tests miss.
The practical takeaway is clear: training that emphasizes speed and explosiveness—alongside traditional strength work—may offer an underappreciated lever for extending both lifespan and healthspan.

Vioxx (rofecoxib), a COX-2 selective painkiller launched by Merck in 1999, became one of the biggest drug-safety scandals of the modern era. Marketed as an arthritis and pain treatment with fewer gastrointestinal side effects than traditional NSAIDs like naproxen, it quickly became a blockbuster, with annual sales exceeding $2 billion and roughly 20 million Americans (and more than 80 million people worldwide) taking it before its withdrawal. 
Internal Merck documents show the company had indications of cardiovascular risks years earlier. Memos from the mid-to-late 1990s discussed potential increases in thrombotic events linked to the drug’s mechanism. The 2000 VIGOR trial (versus naproxen) revealed a substantially higher rate of heart attacks on Vioxx. On March 9, 2000, Merck research chief Edward Scolnick emailed colleagues that the cardiovascular events “are clearly there,” calling it a “shame” and “mechanism-based as we worried it was.” Public statements at the time often attributed the difference to a protective effect of naproxen or emphasized a favorable profile, while internal discussions considered reformulation ideas and study designs that might minimize unflattering comparisons. Merck disclosed data to the FDA and later added label warnings, but the drug stayed on the market amid aggressive marketing. 
The decisive public evidence came in 2004 from the placebo-controlled APPROVe trial (for colon polyps), which showed roughly double the rate of heart attacks and strokes after about 18 months. Merck voluntarily withdrew Vioxx worldwide on September 30, 2004. Estimates of harm, including a widely cited Lancet analysis, put U.S. excess heart attacks in the tens of thousands (around 88,000 with roughly 38,000 deaths in one model), though figures vary. 
The aftermath featured tens of thousands of lawsuits. Merck, without admitting liability, settled most personal-injury claims for $4.85 billion in 2007 and paid additional sums in regulatory and investor resolutions. The episode highlighted gaps in post-marketing surveillance, the role of marketing in shaping scientific presentation, and the challenge of balancing GI benefits against cardiovascular risks—prompting tighter scrutiny of COX-2 inhibitors and greater emphasis on cardiovascular safety trials for new pain drugs.
